body:
`--set` makes this impossible to override. `--set-default` still disables automatic updates by default but leaves the escape hatch.

```suggestion
            postFixup = "wrapProgram $out/bin/fx --set-default FX_AUTO_UPGRADE 0";
```

I _think_ this isn't necessary because nixpkgs is pinned by flake.lock, but I think this is a suitable suggestion, so feel free to correct me if I'm wrong regarding nixpkgs already being pinned, in which case I'm happy to accept.
IMO this adds maintenance burden, so I won't accept instantly. Feel free to push back, but the goal of the PR is to make maintenance as frictionless as possible for the Vercel team.

**[P1] Avoid partial in-place restoration**

When atomic replacement fails because the parent directory is not writable, this fallback writes preimage bytes directly over the live file before knowing the write will finish. A disk-full, RLIMIT, or device error after a partial write leaves the file’s prefix replaced even though `setLength` is never reached. That violates the safety invariant and can still destroy user data. Please fail the undo instead of falling back in-place, or provide a rollback mechanism, and add a test combining the locked-directory path with a mid-stream failure.

**[P2] Report restoration failures as unavailable**

The delete/write/edit restoration catches still free `op.path` and return `.empty`, so `/undo` reports “Nothing to undo” after consuming an operation that failed. This contradicts the new `UndoResult.unavailable` contract and hides the I/O failure. Please return `.unavailable = op.path` for these failures and after a successfully rolled-back rename.

**[P1] Pin sessions before releasing the registry lock**

Copying `self.sessions` only snapshots raw pointers; it does not pin the sessions. After the mutex is released, a still-running client can recycle a reference-zero slot and destroy the evicted session before this loop calls `session.shutdown()`. Because this path specifically runs while clients remain active, that recreates the use-after-free class the PR is meant to eliminate. Please retain/pin each session under the lock, or transition the registry into a state that prevents recycling, before shutting them down.

**[P1] Include the actual shell invocation semantics**

`environment: user` and `/bin/bash` still omit the behavior that makes #237 exploitable. Fx actually executes `/bin/bash --login -O expand_aliases -c ...` or `/bin/zsh -l -i -c ...`; a reviewer given only `/bin/bash` can reasonably model ordinary `bash -c`, where aliases are disabled. The evidence nevertheless remains marked complete. Please serialize the exact invocation argv/startup flags—ideally derived from `capturedInvocation`—and test that the payload includes the login and alias-expansion semantics.

**[P1] Wire the goal context into production dispatch**

`goal_ctx` defaults to null and no production construction site populates it; only the goal callbacks read it. Since all three tools are advertised globally, every shipped invocation currently returns “goal tools unavailable.” Please create and own the per-session context in the runtime dispatch path, with an integration test through the real tool registry.

**[P1] Persist mutations produced by the goal tools**

`handleCreate` and `handleUpdate` serialize their `SetOutcome` and then deinitialize it. `callCreate`/`callUpdate` return only that JSON, so no new goal is transferred to or persisted by the host. Even after `goal_ctx` is populated, a subsequent `get_goal` will still see the original state. Please add a mutation sink or callback and persist the new goal before returning success.

**[P1] Do not report success for a no-op slash command**

This path validates the objective and prints “Goal set,” but it never calls `goal_service.set` or stores anything. Status, clear, pause, and resume are likewise hard-coded as if no goal exists. `/goal` is therefore entirely nonfunctional and misleading. Please wire it to the live and durable session state before reporting success.

**[P1] Integrate accounting and steering with turn execution**

`accountProgress`, the usage/time accounting methods, and all three steering-prompt functions have no production callers. Nothing counts turn usage, changes a goal to `budget_limited`, injects continuation, or persists the updated counters. Please connect these at the turn boundary and add an end-to-end lifecycle test.

**[P2] Reset identity and accounting for a new objective**

Replacing a terminal goal duplicates the previous record and changes only its objective, status, budget, and update time. It retains the old `goal_id`, `tokens_used`, `time_used_seconds`, and `created_at_ms`, so a new objective can begin already over budget. Please create a fresh goal record with a new ID and zeroed accounting while retaining the previous snapshot separately.

**[P1] Add build and install phases**

This derivation never runs `zig build` and never installs a binary. With no Makefile, the generic phases do nothing; `postInstall` only installs license files, then `postFixup` attempts to wrap nonexistent `$out/bin/fx`. Add explicit build/install phases and a check that executes `$out/bin/fx --version`.

**[P1] Stream the response instead of buffering it**

`Client.fetch` drains the entire response into `body` before `consumeSse` runs. Content and tool callbacks therefore wait until xAI closes the response, cancellation cannot interrupt a stalled stream, and the allocating writer has no response-size bound. Feed a streaming reader to an incremental SSE decoder with a cancellation watcher.

**[P1] Preserve every streamed tool-call index**

The request enables `parallel_tool_calls`, but this parser only reads `calls[0]`, while `consumeSse` uses one global id/name/arguments accumulator and ignores `tool_call_index`. Multiple tool calls are dropped or merged. Accumulate every array entry by index and add a two-call regression.

**[P1] Make Chat Completions reads cancellable**

After the bounded open, `receiveHead` and the SSE reader perform blocking reads with only before/after flag checks. If a server stops sending, Escape cannot close the socket and the turn can hang indefinitely. Install the equivalent of the Responses path’s HTTP cancellation watcher around send, head, and body reads.

**[P1] Do not turn an incomplete EOF into success**

`.eof` is treated like `[DONE]`, then any partial content or tools are assigned `.stop`/`.tool_calls`. A connection closing after one delta is therefore committed as a successful turn without terminal evidence. Return an incomplete/read failure on bare EOF without a finish reason and add a content-delta-plus-EOF regression.

**[P1] Heap-own the state that surviving threads reference**

Skipping `deinit` does not keep these objects alive: `state`, `persistent_store`, and `registry` are locals in `runSupported`. When it returns, detached client threads retain dangling `&state` and `&registry` pointers. Heap-allocate and intentionally leak the shared allocation on timeout, or wait until every client thread stops.

**[P1] Enforce `as_parsed` for zsh too**

This only disables Bash alias expansion. zsh still runs with `-l -i -c`, allowing `.zshrc` aliases/functions to rewrite auto-allowlisted command words on the default macOS shell. Make `as_parsed` bypass zsh user definitions too, or execute the resolved program directly, and add a zsh alias regression.

**[P1] Read the finished payload under the mutex**

`markFinished` publishes the result, flags, model arrays, and `finished` under `turn.mutex`, but this path reads them without that lock or an atomic publication primitive. This is a data race and can observe `finished` without a synchronized payload. Expose a locked finished-result snapshot or equivalent acquire/release publication.

**[P1] Join the detached warmup before destroying App**

The detached job retains pointers to the App-owned `SessionStore` and `Host.ctx`, but shutdown does not track or join it. Skipping session destruction while busy cannot keep the stack field or App alive. Exiting during an npx warmup leaves the worker using dangling pointers. Track and cancel/join the warmup, or heap-own its shared state.

**[P1] Do not salvage transport read failures as completed output**

`ReadFailed` is collapsed into clean stream termination, after which earlier text or parseable tool arguments become `.stop`/`.tool_calls`. A connection dying midway through a later event silently commits truncated output. Preserve transport-failure state and limit salvage to proven clean EOF/`[DONE]`; add a valid-delta-plus-partial-event regression.

**[P1] Do not override an explicit SSE retry interval**

This changes a server-supplied `retry: 500` into 1000 ms. Full CI confirms the regression: MCP conformance `ClientRespectsRetryField` fails because reconnection occurs at about 1002 ms instead of 500 ms. Preserve explicit retry values and apply a default/backoff only when the field is absent, or address the storm outside the protocol hint.

Addressed in 583b7a5. `ReadFailed` now propagates as a transport failure; only clean EOF or `[DONE]` reaches the usable-output salvage. I also added a regression with a valid text delta, a buffered partial later event, and `ReadFailed`. The PR description now states that the live proxy close remains unreproduced, so this change does not conflate that uncertainty with clean termination.

> Preserve explicit retry values and apply a default/backoff only when the field is absent, or address the storm outside the protocol hint.

Done in 8076f9e, on top of your 4057030b. The wait is a default rather than a floor now: `retry_ms > 0` is used as the server sent it, and the one second applies only when there is no hint, which is the case #301 came from.

I reproduced your failure locally before touching anything, then confirmed the fix against the same runner: `sse-retry` on 2025-11-25 gave `Client reconnected very late (1003ms instead of 500ms)`, and now reports `client-sse-retry-timing SUCCESS` with the GET landing 504ms after the stream close. Full suite is 471 passed, 0 failed.

Worth flagging on your commit, since I rebased over it rather than replacing it. Lowering the floor to 500 clears the check but leaves the override in place below that. I ran the fixture with a 200ms hint against both builds:

| | observed gaps |
|---|---|
| 4057030b | 501, 501, 500, 501, 501, 500 |
| 8076f9e | 200, 201, 201, 200, 201 |

The suite passes at 500 because its `retryValue` is 500 and the floor was set to the same number. At `retry: 200` its very-late threshold is 400ms, so a 501ms reconnect would fail it. That is what pushed me to honor the field instead of picking a floor value.

Two things to sanity-check on your side. I put the no-hint default back to one second, since once the hint is honored that constant only governs servers that sent nothing; say the word if you want 500 there. And I inverted `retry_hint_listener`, which previously sent `retry: 1` and asserted it got clamped, so it now sends the suite's own 500 and bounds the observed spacing on both sides. Measured 501ms across seven reconnects. That puts the regression in `mcp-legacy-remote` rather than only in Full CI, which is why my default check rollup was green while this was broken.

The no-hint storm cases are unchanged and still fail without the default: 0ms listener spacing and 9519 resume requests. Each call site is covered separately, the listener by the e2e test and the resume path by conformance, and I checked that by clamping one site at a time.

Tool-result messages in the Claude Messages request are not valid JSON: the `.tool` branch closes the `tool_result` object and the `content` array, but never closes the outer message object. This will produce malformed payloads whenever tool results are sent back to Claude.

This issue also appears on line 250 of the same file.

This changelog entry says Claude uses the Messages API for interactive sessions, but the Claude provider implementation routes interactive streaming through the local Claude Code CLI by default (HTTP Messages is only used in specific paths like e2e override / permission reviewer). The release notes should match the actual transport used.

README claims the fx-owned Claude session (stored at `~/.fx/claude-auth.json`) is used as a fallback when Claude Code isn't signed in, but the current Claude stream provider always uses the local `claude` CLI unless an e2e override is set. Either implement the documented fallback or adjust the README to avoid implying inference works without the Claude Code CLI.

> Please retain/pin each session under the lock, or transition the registry into a state that prevents recycling, before shutting them down.

Fixed in efda37e. `shutdownSessionsOnly` now takes a reference on every live session while the registry mutex is held, signals them after releasing it, then gives the references back. Recycling already skips a referenced slot, so this reuses the registry's own mechanism rather than adding a second one.

Two tests, each checked against the mistake it covers: the references return to zero once the drain finishes, so a leaked pin cannot wedge a later `removeOwned` that waits on the count, and a referenced slot is not recycled while the same slots recycle once the references drop.

> Skipping `deinit` does not keep these objects alive: `state`, `persistent_store`, and `registry` are locals in `runSupported`. When it returns, detached client threads retain dangling `&state` and `&registry` pointers.

You are right, and the comment I left there was wrong about what skipping `deinit` buys. Fixed in 93b16a6: the three now live in one heap-allocated `Shared`, handed out as pointers that outlive the frame, freed as a group only once the drain confirms no client thread is left, and deliberately left behind otherwise.

Chasing it turned up two more things the registry holds that have the same problem, both on the path this PR added:

- `host_identity` pointed at `host_instance`, a `[32]u8` array in the frame.
- `durable_root` and `transport_root` pointed into `paths`, and `defer paths.deinit(alloc)` is not gated on the drain the way the store and registry teardown is. So on exactly the path that keeps the registry alive for surviving clients, `Paths.deinit` freed the two strings the registry still points at. That one is a read of freed memory rather than a stale frame pointer.

`Shared` owns copies of all three, so the whole group the registry can reach is either reclaimed together or kept together.

One detail worth naming: the error cleanup lives in `Shared.init` as `errdefer` rather than in `runSupported`. An `errdefer` in the caller would also fire on later error returns, once clients are running, which would free the state out from under them. Inside `init` the only reachable errors are before the host accepts anything.

Suite is unchanged against the branch head: 8339/8395 before, 8340/8396 after, same 34 failed and 7 crashed, and the named failures are an identical set of 41. The extra test and pass is the one below.

On testing, I want to be straight about the limit. I could not write a test that goes RED on the original defect: reading a dead stack frame is undefined rather than deterministically wrong, so it would pass or fail by luck. What is covered deterministically is the ownership: the registry's three slices are copies rather than aliases of `paths`, they point into the group, and `deinit` returns every one of them to the allocator. The dangling-frame half is structural, and I would rather say so than imply coverage I do not have.

Each of those assertions was checked against the mistake it covers: dropping any one of the four frees leaks, and aliasing any of the three slices instead of copying it fails. The identity one is why that matters, since it passed until I made the test hand in a caller-owned buffer the way `runSupported` does rather than a literal.

> Please fail the undo instead of falling back in-place, or provide a rollback mechanism, and add a test combining the locked-directory path with a mid-stream failure.

Fixed in ff9e981. `restoreContent` is `writeFileAtomic` and nothing else now, so a file whose directory denies writes is refused rather than overwritten in place, and the caller reports the refusal. The docstring says why, since the absence of a fallback is the point and easy to add back by accident.

Two tests cover it: undo on a locked directory leaves the file byte-for-byte intact and reports that it could not act, and the locked-directory path combined with a failing write never leaves a half-replaced file.

> Please return `.unavailable = op.path` for these failures and after a successfully rolled-back rename.

Done in ff9e981 for the three sites you named: the delete and write/edit restore failures, and the rename that gets rolled back after its displaced file cannot be put back.

Reading the rest of `undoLast` for the same invariant turned up three more, fixed in 929e882. Two of them are louder than the ones you flagged, because they reported success rather than an empty stack:

- A rename whose move back fails returned `.empty`, so `/undo` printed "Nothing to undo" over an I/O failure on an operation it had already consumed. That is the symptom you described, at a path the list did not reach.
- A new file that could not be deleted swallowed the error and returned `.deleted`, telling the user a file was removed while it is still on disk.
- A rename recorded without its `new_path`, which happens when duplicating that path fails, returned `.restored` without renaming anything.

One carve-out worth stating, because my first attempt got it wrong. A file that is already gone still counts as `.deleted`: absent is the end state undo wants there, and returning `.unavailable` for it would be a false failure. Only other errors are treated as failures. The existing already-absent test is what caught that and now pins it.

Each changed branch was checked against the mistake it covers. Reverting the rename-back path to `.empty`, the delete to a swallowed catch, and the missing `new_path` to `.restored` each turn their test red, and dropping the `FileNotFound` carve-out turns the already-absent test red.

The third one is my call rather than your ask, so push back if you would rather leave it: `new_path` is only ever null after an allocation failure, so it is narrow, but `.restored` for a rename that never happened contradicts the contract this PR introduces.

Addressed in 43b37e6. The checked-in deterministic TUI E2E now drives the built binary through create_goal, a finalized turn, automatic continuation, update_goal completion, and a second finalized turn. It asserts the continuation prompt contains persisted first-turn usage, final usage increases after completion, status persists as complete, and stderr is empty. `bun test tui-slash-commands.test.ts` passes with 11 tests and 0 failures.

You were still right about this one, and I was wrong to say it was done.

Honoring the hint fixed the stream that carried it and nothing after. `retry_ms`
is rebuilt per attempt in `readNotificationStream` and `readSseStream`, so the
value never survived into the next reconnect, and the retry field sets the
reconnection time until the server changes it rather than for one stream. A
server that sends `retry: 500` once and then omits it got 500ms on the first
reconnect and our 1000ms on every one after. I changed the fixture to send the
hint once and measured 1004ms, against the ~1002ms you originally reported. Same
substitution, one reconnect later.

The reason neither of us saw it is that `retry_hint_listener` repeats the field
on every response, so no fixture in the file could express a hint that stops
arriving. Dropping the stickiness now turns the new test red and leaves the old
one green, which is what the gap looked like.

The resume path had the same shape and no hint coverage at all: the only fixture
emitting a hint sat in the GET branch, so a floor or an override at that call
site passed all four tests. Overriding it now fails only the new test.

Fixed in ca4979a2 and a466e428, on top of your 4057030b:

- the interval is held across attempts at both call sites
- `retry_hint_once` covers a hint sent once and then omitted
- `retry_hint_resume` covers the resume path's hint branch
- the delay decision moved into one function both loops call, with a unit test,
  since two copies with one of them untested is how this got through

Two judgment calls worth your disagreement.

The first reconnect no longer waits when there is no hint. An ordinary stream
that closes after delivering its work was paying a full second: the three
per-version resume tests ran in 3.41s against 558ms without the delay, and the
2025-11-25 polling test 1139ms against 143ms. The default from the second
reconnect onward is what bounds the storm, and removing it still turns both
storm tests red. I did not gate on whether the attempt delivered events, which
was my first instinct, because the resume-storm server sends a progress
notification every time it closes and that gate would have reopened #301.

An explicit `retry: 0` falls back to the default rather than being honored
literally, since zero wait is the defect. Say the word if you would rather it be
honored as sent.

I also did not add a lower bound on small hints. `retry: 1` still reconnects at
that rate, unchanged from before this PR, but every bound I could write is an
override of an explicit interval, which is the thing you asked me not to do.
Happy to take it in a separate change if you want it.

Conformance is unchanged at 484 passed / 5 failed, with the same
`sep-2322-client-request-state` that also fails on an unmodified `main` here.
`mcp-legacy-remote` is 46/0 against 39/0 on the base. The branch is rebased onto
current `main`; CI on the new head has not finished yet.

Retained slots have an age limit but no idle TTL. After the session idles past a NAT/proxy timeout the socket is silently dead: this ping's write succeeds, the pong read blocks, and the turn stalls until the event-idle watcher fires (default 30s) before reconnecting. An idle TTL (~5 min, matching codex-rs and pi) avoids that, and with it this per-reuse ping — a blocking RTT on every reused turn — could probably go too, or at least get its own short deadline (~2s) instead of the 30s idle timeout.

`shutdown()` deinits busy slots too, closing and freeing a `Connection` a streaming thread may still hold. Related: the two relock sites in `acquire` (the ping-failure path and the post-connect commit) index `slots.items[slot_index]` without the length check that `release`/`continuation`/`rollbackReservation` do — after this swap that's an out-of-bounds index. Skipping busy slots here (`release` already closes the connection when `index >= slots.items.len`) and adding the bounds checks covers both.

When can `health_failures < health_budget` be false here? Both increment paths (`release(.failed)`, the ping failure below) also null `slot.connection`, and `release(.completed)` resets to 0 — so an idle slot with a live connection always has 0 failures. If it's future-proofing, fine; if it's meant to poison a flapping lane it doesn't currently do that.

`acquire`'s entry check returns `error.Timeout` when the request deadline already expired, with delivery still `definitely_unsent` — so a turn that just ran out of time latches the whole process to SSE. Same when a short request deadline bounds the connect instead of the transport's own timeout. Worth latching only when the transport's own connect timeout fired.

This reads exactly one frame, so a server ping or trailing data frame between our close and its close reply returns `WebSocketProtocolViolation`. `close()` swallows it, but the one-shot `stream()` propagates it — failing a turn whose response was already fully consumed. Looping until the close frame arrives (answering pings, discarding data) matches RFC 6455 here.
Seems like AI coding agent leakage :) You should remove this from the PR
@fazxes I'm not sure how good this is for Zig code. It's all vibed. Feel free to fix it.

With the bridge active, `fixed_scope` replaces `requestedScope` entirely, so `options.config.scopes` and `previous_scope` are never read for the fx Slack client. Verified by building this branch: `scopes: ["channels:read"]` in `mcp.json` produced a request for all twelve fx.sh scopes, including `chat:write`, `files:write` and `users:write`. Existing tokens are unaffected, but the next reauthorization asks for write permissions the user never configured, and the local `scopes` key becomes inert without saying so.

If fx-web #130 accepts a subset, this could intersect `options.config.scopes` with the published list when the user configured any, and fall back to the full list otherwise. That keeps read-only setups possible.

This makes fx.sh a hard dependency for authenticating Slack with the fx client id, where localhost worked on its own before. Reasonable for an internal flow, but worth one line in the body, since the error a user sees is `SlackBridgeUnavailable` rather than anything pointing at fx.sh.

Addressed the silent permission expansion in [390c7ff7](https://github.com/vercel-labs/fx/commit/390c7ff7b0d1d31d463f095c6a2ad05a772263d5). We are retaining the fixed nine-scope set shared with fx-web #130, so read-only subsets remain unsupported. An explicit local scope list that omits any shared scope, including an empty list, now stops authorization before the browser opens and explains the policy. Configuration and stored credentials remain unchanged. With no override, the CLI requests the shared set; a configured superset requests only the shared set. Regression coverage includes read-only and empty lists, reauthorization, credential preservation, and the in-session explanation. All 26 focused authentication tests pass locally.

Documented this in the PR body's Rollout section and the README: new personal authorization and reauthorization for the Fx Slack Client ID require fx.sh, unavailable metadata returns `SlackBridgeUnavailable`, and there is no localhost fallback for Fx. The rollout instructions require deploying fx-web #130 first and retaining the registered localhost callback for older clients. Other Slack Client IDs and MCP providers retain their direct callback behavior without contacting fx.sh.
